text:
maya: FYI - saw a consistent delta in prefix hit-rate between us-east and eu-west after yesterday's kernel swap. eu-west cold-region misses jumped ~4.5% at 00:12 UTC.

ezra: when you say kernel swap do you mean the new int8 execution path? :thinking_face:

maya: yep. rolled the optimized attention kernels to canary-prod at 00:05 and then to all-serving at 00:10. latencies OK, but regional KV hit-rate dropped in eu-west.

lin: could be cache key normalization differences + different sequence-length distributions. sim traffic we used was mostly shorter sequences so the new kernel's batching changed the grouping behavior.

jess: +1. I dug into the logs, looks like a subtle keying mismatch from prompt canonicalization. sample from the logs: 
```
CACHE_MISS key="user:pref:7f3a:prompt_v1::len=128" region=eu-west model=gptx-int8
CACHE_HIT key="user:pref:7f3a:prompt_v1::len=64" region=us-east model=gptx-int8
```
We accidentally include tokenized-length in the cache key when kernel batching pads/truncates differently per backend.

maya: ugh. so same user/prefix ends up with different keys depending on runtime padding heuristics. explains the fragmentation.

ezra: where is the padding decided? runtime-level or kernel-level? If kernel picks a different internal pad-length for int8, key divergence makes sense.

lin: kernel chooses internal tile sizes for attention which influences the effective sequence-length it asks for. previously all runtimes rounded to multiples of 8, new kernel rounds to 16 for performance.

jess: quick mitigation: normalize the cache key upstream to use logical seq_len (the requested length) not the kernel pad_len. proposal patch in PR: 
```
# cache_key.py
def make_cache_key(prefix_hash, request_len, model_tag):
    seq_bucket = (request_len + 31) // 32 * 32  # coarse bucketing
    return f"{prefix_hash}:{model_tag}:len={seq_bucket}"
```
This reduces key cardinality and tolerates pad differences.

maya: nice. any perf tradeoffs? coarser buckets may slightly reduce hit quality but should massively increase hit-rate on warmup.

rajesh: can we run sim traffic that replicates the kernel-level padding? Right now our warmup generator uses token counts, not pad strategy. Suggest we add a padding emulator.

lin: I built a tiny simulator that replays padding behaviors across kernels. Short result: if pads differ (8->16) we lose 2-6% effective hit-rate on a 100k prefix sample. With bucketing we recover ~90% of that.

ops-bot: deploy queued by maya:deploy/warmup-key-normalize (staging) — started 2065432200

jess: also found routing policy interaction: requests routed by cost-tier pick eu-west small instances that call a fallback kernel variant which pads differently. So routing+kernel swap = compounding effect.

maya: good catch. we should add a routing rule that prefers homogeneous kernel families during rollout windows. short-term: add a canary tag to avoid mixing kernel families for same customer IDs.

ezra: for warmup strategy: propose we do three-phase approach - 1) normalize keys asap, 2) run targeted synthetic warmup that mimics kernel pad sizes per region + model variant, 3) measure and adjust routing to avoid mixed-kernel fanout.

jess: agreed. I'll open a small PR for key normalization and a playbook for region-specific simulated warmup.

lin: also recommend an alert: if regional hit-rate delta > 1.5% for 10m -> auto-suspend cross-region splitting for that model/version.

maya: capture action items: 
- jess: PR for cache key normalization (staging)
- jess/lin: warmup sim that accounts for kernel pad behavior, run against eu-west and us-east (today)
- maya: routing-canary policy to prevent mixed-kernel fanout during rollouts
- ops: monitor and rollback threshold (lin's delta alert)

rajesh: I'll schedule a short perf run at 21:00 UTC with synthetic traces that include the larger-seq tails. will share metrics. :+1:

maya: thanks all — this explains the regression. keep updates here. :eyes:
